And why would they give the Lord lame, sick, and blind sheep? For the same reason they gave moldy bread. To give God something that they really didn't want anyway. Give them not their best. And you know, the things of the Lord come last. Whereas the things of the Lord should come first. We need to be hot. Not lukewarm for the Lord. And then you go down to verse 13. Not that we necessarily want to be uh known as somebody that's often left field. But the problem is the world will regard us that way if we're serving the Lord. And we don't want to be ashamed of the Lord. Well, a son honors his father. We need to honor our father. We need to be hot for him. We need to be wholehearted in our service for the Lord. And not half-hearted, not lukewarm. Let's bow in prayer. O Lord, we pray that thou would bless these thoughts to our hearts. And O Lord, we pray that we would not be lukewarm We pray that we would not be half-hearted. We pray that we would not be halfway there. And, O Lord, we pray that we might serve thee with our whole heart and mind and soul and body And just forgive us for what we fall short of that in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.text: So this being Reformation uh Sunday and also the communion service, I thought it would be good if we uh looked at uh what the uh Lord's Supper means in the scriptures and particularly as it was brought back uh into alignment by the Reformers Uh the Catholic Church had greatly mangled the uh communion service into an offense, and the reformers said, well, here's the Word of God and here is what it teaches This week, the 31st of October, is the 502nd anniversary of Martin Luther nailing his 95 theses on the church door in Wittenberg uh which was uh the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. But what is not quite as well known is that this year, 2019, marks the 500th anniversary of the famous Leipzig debate between Luther and Johann Eck, who was an apologist for Rome and who was a great debater. And it was during this debate that uh uh Luther really sealed his fate. He uh had the audacity to declare that he didn't believe in the authority of the Pope Uh and uh uh when they asked why, well I don't find the the Pope mentioned in the scriptures anywhere. And then he also um declared uh sola scriptura, which is the theme of the Reformation, uh, that our Christian faith and beliefs are based solely on the Word of God, and thus only Scripture He also declared that indulgences, uh he condemned the indulgences whereby people could uh throw some money into the box and uh release themselves from uh certain numbers of years of uh purgatory. And this was a cash cow for the Catholic Church. Uh here were poor people that could hardly uh make a living and take care of their families and they were uh in fear, constant fear that they weren't good enough and so they would uh put their hard earned money in and the Pope and his minions uh lived in luxury in Rome and uh they uh also uh needed this money for the uh building of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, which is a a beautiful uh world uh architecture, but nonetheless it was built on the backs of of people that could barely feed themselves. And so after all of this, after this debate, the Pope issued a papal bull, which was a statement condemning Luther's writings and forbidding them And uh this put Luther into great peril. This was uh in the the Bible from the beginning, but uh he restored uh this uh biblical teaching from the abuse of Rome. sermons.title: "A Godly Revolution"
sermons.speaker: Pastor Ken Olsen
sermons.text: Good morning. I don't think I've ever watched a presidential debate because it's mainly the two people attacking each other, but It seems like that debate this past week went pretty well and uh showed up uh a little bit of the right and wrong there, which is good Let's turn our Bibles to Exodus. Exodus chapter 2. And today we want to look at the 4th of July. Actually, Exodus chapter 1. We want to look at the things having to do with the independence of America and a godly revolution that was had back in 1776. It was a godly revolution. Now we just read this morning from Romans 13. The great passage about the Christian and the government. And we're going to look at 1 Peter, which has to do with that same thing. And when you read that those passages on the surface, they seem to indicate that you should always obey your government and you should always be subject And period. But no, that's not what we have in the Bible. And it has there in that passage in Romans chapter 13, he is the minister of God to thee for good. Is our government the minister of God to us for good today? In a lot of ways it's not. And was the government of King George back In the time of the colonies, was it a minister of God to them for good? Well they definitely had determined that he was not a government uh minister of God to them for good And it was a godly revolution of godly people there at July fourth, seventeen seventy-six, when they signed the Declaration of Independence And you know, you have to look at the context of the revolution. And the context was the Great Awakening. And just before the American Revolution, you had the Great Awakening, and there was a great revival in America. Jonathan Edwards, you had uh George Whitfield, you had the tenants, you had a uh many godly men preaching godly things And the people were getting saved in Jonathan Edwards Church. They were grabbing the pillars of the church, not wanting to sink into hell because God was convicting them so much And that's the context right before the American Revolution. And these were godly men at the time of the American Revolution. And they made that revolution. And so what we want to see about obeying the government all the time and in every circumstance, we don't have that taught in the Bible. And if you go back to Exodus chapter 1, Exodus chapter 1 and verse 15. We have the Hebrew midwives. And here we have Exodus 1. 15, and the king of Egypt spake to the Hebrew midwives, of which the name of the one was Shifra, in the name of the other Pu'ah. And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools, if it be a son, then ye shall kill him. But if it be a daughter, then ye shall then she shall live. But the midwives feared God and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive. You notice they did not obey Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, for they are or actually verse 18, we forgot that. And the king of Egypt Called for the midwives and said unto them, Why have ye done this thing and have saved the men and children alive? And the wiz midwives said to Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, for they are lively and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them. Therefore, God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and waxed very mighty, and it came to pass because the midwives feared God that he made them houses. And so here we have the midwives. They did not obey Pharaoh. They did not obey the ruler. They did not obey the government to kill the Hebrew boys. And they saved them alive. They gave an excuse for it that didn't hold much water. But anyway, they saved them alive. They obeyed God and didn't commit murder. And it says the end result, verse 20, therefore God blessed them. God blessed them. God made them houses, made them big families. Because they obeyed God rather than men. Remember back with Peter and the Apostles in the book of Acts, well, they said we ought to obey God rather than men. And that's what these Hebrew midwives did. You know, back in World War Two, they had the Nuremberg trials, remember, of the Nazi war criminals criminals And what was the defense of the Nazi war criminals back in Nuremberg and just after World War II? Well, their defense was, oh, we did all these atrocities because we were ordered to do it. And therefore it was all right. We were ordered to do it Well, the midwives were ordered to kill the men children, and they didn't do it. They disobeyed the government. And the Nazis should have disobeyed as well. And then we go on back to another example of this to get started here today. We go back to 1 Samuel. 1 Samuel chapter 22. 1 Samuel chapter 22. And we have some more people that disobeyed the government. 1 Samuel 22, and then verse 9. Then answered Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, and said, I saw the son of Jesse, that's David, coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahita, the priest. And he inquired of the Lord for him and gave him bittles and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine. Do you ever remember hearing on the Beverly Hillbillies about bittles? Granny talking about the bittles Well, that's what it is right here. That comes right from the King James Bible, Vittles, verse 10. And so the priest gave him vitals, gave him the sword of Goliath Then verse 11, and the king sent to call Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests that were in Nob, and they came all of them to the king. And Saul said, Hear now, thou son of Ahitab. And he answered, I, here I am, my lord. And Saul said unto him, Why have ye considered Conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread and a sword, and hast inquired of God for him, that he should rise against me to lie in wait as at this day Then Ahimelech the priest answered the king and said, And who is so faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king's son-in-law, and goeth at thy bidding and is honorable in my house Did I then begin to inquire of God for him? Be it far from me. Let not the king impute anything unto his servant, nor to all the house of my father, for thy servant knew nothing of all this. Less or more. And so here the priest said he didn't know that David was running away from Saul. In verse 16, and the king said, Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou and all thy father's house. And the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, the soldiers there, Turn and slay the priests of the Lord, because their hand also is with David, and because they knew when he fled and did not show it to me. But the servants of the king would not Put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord. And the king said to Doad, Turn thou and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned and he fell upon the priests and slew on that day four score and five persons that did wear a linen ephi. And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen and asses and sheep with the edge of the sword. So here we have another good example in the Bible of people that did not obey the government. They did not obey the king. You know, back in those days, the king's word was law. Back with Louis XIV, the king in France, he said, the state is me and I am the state. And that's how it was with kings back then. And yet, when the king commanded his soldiers there to kill the priests, what did they do? They resisted. They would not kill the priests They would not do it, even though that was with the orders. And they got some foreigner there who had given the report about David, Doeg the Edomite, they got him to do it So anyway, the just following orders defense doesn't work. It doesn't work in the Bible. And here we have examples of people that disobeyed the government. And now let's go all the way back to 1 Peter. 1 Peter, 1 Peter chapter 2, and here's a parallel passage to Romans chapter 13. And this parallel passage starts with verse 5 13, verse 13 of chapter 2 of 1 Peter. And Jehoiada the high priest saved the child Joash, and when he was seven years old, he was presented to the people, and they had a revolution, a godly revolution And they were there with their swords, they were ready to fight, and they said, God saved the king, God saved Joash and Jehoiada, the godly uh priest of the Lord, he put Joash on the throne. And Athaliah actually was killed. And we have all kinds of uh examples of godly revolutions in the past. There was a godly revolution in England with Cromwell Cromwell, they put down the king, Charles I, and it was basically the beginning of democratic government in our modern world with Cromwell back in the 1600s in England. And so there are limits to things. And so we want to look at a few of these things and a few of the godly people that what they have had to say about. These matters. Anybody ever hear of Robert L. Dabney? Dabney. Well, Dabney, he was the chaplain of Stonewall Jackson. And he was a great theologian, wrote books of theology, taught in the seminary, taught in the University of Virginia. And he was a great Christian, great Presbyterian, and he said about limited authority, he says, again we have seen that sovereignty is in the people rather than the rulers. May the people never resume their own when it is wholly abused to their injury, when the power is, they're abused by that power There may be obviously a point, then, where resistance to tyrants is obedience to God. And that's what Robert L. Dabney said, great theologian of the Presbyterian Church. And then Charles Hodge. Probably heard of him, wrote the big systematic theology books of the Presbyterians, taught at uh Princeton Seminary. But anyway, he talked about limited authority back in the 1800s He said, a father, if he shamefully abuses his power, may rightfully be deprived of authority over his children. If he abuses his authority, the father may be limited in his power over the children. And then John Knox. John Knox was a great figure of church history in Scotland, a beater of the Reformation there. And he was he had a continual battle with Mary, Queen of Scots, and with uh government back then. And so as he stood before Queen Mary, he said For no greater honor is to be given to kings than God has committed to be given to father and mother. But the father may be struck with a frenzy in which he would slay his children. Now, madame, talking to the queen there. If the children arise, join together, apprehend their father, take his sword from him, bind his hands, keep him in prison till the frenzy is over, think you, madame, that the children do any wrong? Even so, madam, it is with the princes that would murder the children of God that are subject to them. They must be resisted, and that's what Martin Luther did. I mean, what uh John Knox did, Martin Luther did the same thing in the church. He resisted the tyranny in the church. Well, that brings us to the American Revolution. And I have a little book here called Presbyterians and the Revolution. I already preached a message here in the past about the Presbyterian Rebellion. It was called the Presbyterian Rebellion in America, the American Revolution. And here we have the uh uh The revolution was back in 1776. They had the Declaration of Independence, and they were debating it in the Constitutional Congress. And they couldn't decide whether to sign it or not to sign it, whether they wanted to declare revolution. It was a big thing And so I read here from this book that was put out a hundred years at the hundred-year anniversary of the American Revolution back in the 1800s. It says, when the Declaration of Independence was under debate, we quote the words of the Reverend Dr. John Krebs, doubts and forebodings were whispered through the hall The house hesitated, wavered, and for a while liberty and slavery appeared to hang in even scale. So here in the Constitutional Congress they were debating the Declaration of Independence. It seemed like it could fail. It was an even scale. It was then that an aged patriot arose, a venerable and stately form, his head white with the frost of years. Remember in Proverbs this morning we looked at the hoary head? Well, this guy had the hoary head. He rose to speak in the Continental Congress there. And there is, said he, a tide in the affairs of men. A nick of time. We perceive it now before us. To hesitate is to consent to our own slavery That noble instrument upon your table, which ensures immortality to its author, should be subscribed this very morning by every pen in the house. And the guy that was speaking was John Witherspoon. He was a Presbyterian preacher, the only preacher in the Continental Congress. And he rose to speak about the Declaration of Independence. He later on went on to be the moderator of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in the United States And then he goes on. For my own part of property I have some, of reputation more. That reputation is staked, that property is pledged on the issue of this contest. And although these grey hairs must st soon descend into the sepulchre, I would infinitely rather that they descend thither by the hand of the executioner then desert at this crisis the sacred cause of my country. And so John Witherspoon, his speech before the Continental Congress, that Presbyterian preacher A godly man, he said that they should sign the Declaration of Independence, and that speech he gave did quite a bit to sway them to sign the Declaration of Independence. And by the way, I think I've mentioned to you before that where I live in Smyrna, I live on Main Street in Smyrna And Main Street in Smyrna has always been, in history, the main north-south highway up the Delmarva Peninsula. He was very, he was a chaplain at Valley Forge. And they're buried there. That just shows how many of the Presbyterians were in the American Revolution and supported it. And then it goes on in this book here. It says that about Presbyterians and the American Revolution. It talks about the battles in the South during the American Revolution, of cow pens, of King's Mountain, they were turning points. And then it says, General Morgan, who commanded at the cow pens, was a Presbyterian elder. General Pickens, who made all the arrangements for the battle, was a Presbyterian elder. And nearly all under their command were Presbyterians in that battle of the American Revolution. In the Battle of King's Mountain, Colonel Campbell, Colonel James Williams, Colonel Cleveland, Colonel Shelby, Colonel Sevier were all Presbyterian elders. And the body of their troops were from Presbyterian settlements. And it was a Presbyterian rebellion. And it was godly men. We know they were godly. Back in those days, just about all the Presbyterians were fundamentalists And they were ones that really believed God and followed him, and they supported the American Revolution. Well, I want to leave you with our final guy, godly man of the revolution, and that was James Caldwell James Caldwell, I'm sure a couple of you have heard of him before. But anyway, he's known as he was a Presbyterian pastor from New Jersey. And he's known as the guy that when there was a battle going on next to his church, the troops, the colonial troops, were running out of wadding for their muskets. They had to have these little pieces of paper wadded up there to make their musket work. James Caldwell had his wife shot and killed there. He had his place burned down. And uh we had a lot of them went to jail, tortured and killed these Presbyterians in the American Revolution, but they paid the price for what they believed And you know, today the attitude is there's nothing really worth fighting for. And so anyway, these men back in the American Revolution, godly men, the Lord led them. They had a godly revolution. sermons.text: We're going to be looking at verses thirteen to twenty-five, picking up where we left off two weeks ago regarding the work that Moses was doing, being led and guided by our Lord Exodus chapter 7, verse 13, we pick up with an affirmative and an absolute statement that's made here in these verses. And he hardened Pharaoh's heart. That he hearken not unto them as the Lord had said. And the Lord said unto Moses, Pharaoh's heart is hardened. He refuses to let the people go. Get thee unto Pharaoh in the morning, lo, he goeth out unto the water, and thou shalt stand by the river's brink against thee come, and the rod which was turned to a serpent shalt thou take in thy hand. And thou shalt say unto him, The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me unto thee, saying, Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness. And behold, hitherto thou wouldest not hear. Thus saith the Lord, In this thou shalt know that I am the Lord. Behold, I will smite with the rod that is in mine hand upon the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood. And the fish that is in the river shall die, and the river shall stink, and the Egyptians shall loathe to drink of the water of the river. And the Lord spake unto Moses, stay unto Aaron, take thy rod, and stretch out thy hand upon the waters of Egypt. upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all the pools of their water, that they may become blood, and there and that there may be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.
